925.title: Duties of the Heart
925.hook: Bahya ibn Paquda teaches that outward practice needs inner work
925.howItsDone: Duties of the Heart is studied in Jewish ethical and spiritual learning, especially in the Musar tradition, and its gate on trust in God is read on its own by some as a guide to bitachon.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kuzari: a devout king told that his intentions were good but his actions were not. Your line was the king asks. Did you ask someone a real question? Today, a book that turns the king's problem inside out. Day nine hundred twenty-five.

A to-do list on the fridge: groceries, call the dentist, return the library book. Every item can be checked off, and by evening the list looks great. But nothing on it says be patient with the kids, or stop resenting your brother, or trust that tomorrow will hold. Those don't fit in a box with a check mark. Yesterday's king had the right intentions and the wrong actions. Today's teacher saw the opposite risk: you can do every right action and leave the heart behind. His name was Bahya ibn Paquda, a judge in Muslim Spain, and his book is called Duties of the Heart.
screen: `A LIST OF THINGS TO CHECK OFF.` → `WHAT DOESN'T FIT IN A BOX.` → `BAHYA'S BOOK.`

segments.voice: Bahya starts by dividing the commandments into two kinds. There are duties of the limbs, things you do with your body: keep the Sabbath, give charity, pray aloud, eat this and not that. And there are duties of the heart, things that happen inside: believing God is one, trusting God, loving God, being humble, being sorry for wrong, examining yourself honestly. In his introduction he says he looked at the books of his day and found long, careful works on the outward duties, and very little on the inner ones. So he wrote this book to fill the gap. One proof text comes from the Shema. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might." Love is not something you can do with your hands. It is a duty of the heart. The same idea sounds in the story of David's anointing, where the prophet is told: "man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart." Bahya organizes the book into gates, one for each inner duty, and one of them is a whole gate on trust. He is not against outward practice. The limbs and the heart need each other. To put it in a picture: a body doing commandments with no heart is like a lamp with no oil; a heart full of good intentions with no deeds is just as incomplete. There is a story in the book: a pious man meets soldiers coming home from battle with their spoils. He tells them they have come back from the lesser war, and now must get ready for the greater one. The greater war is inside: the struggle with your own inclinations. No army can fight that one for you.
screen: `DUTIES OF THE LIMBS.` · `DUTIES OF THE HEART.` · then, large: `THE LORD LOOKETH ON THE HEART.` · `THE LESSER WAR AND THE GREATER WAR.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: do one inner duty. Settle, and let your breath slow. Choose one thing from Bahya's list that nobody can see you do. Trust: hand one worry over, just for these breaths. Humility: remember one thing someone else did better than you, and be glad of it. Self-examination: look honestly at one moment from yesterday. Pick only one. Stay with it. Notice what it's like to do something that leaves no mark on any list. If you pray, you can bring that inner duty into your prayer in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Bahya. A judge in Muslim Spain who wrote Duties of the Heart, teaching that trust, love and humility are commandments too, done inside the heart. Today's word.
Your line: the greater war is inside. Today, add one invisible item to your to-do list, like be patient or trust, and notice when you keep it. Day nine hundred twenty-five.

926.title: Abraham ibn Ezra
926.hook: traveler, poet, grammarian and sharp-eyed commentator
926.howItsDone: Abraham ibn Ezra's commentary is printed alongside the Torah in editions of the Mikraot Gedolot, the rabbinic Bible, and students read him for his attention to grammar and plain meaning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bahya's book, Duties of the Heart: trust, love and humility, the commandments nobody can see. Your line was the greater war is inside. Did you keep one invisible item on your list? Today, a man who couldn't stay put. Day nine hundred twenty-six.

If I sold candles, the sun would never set. That is the gist of a short Hebrew poem, a joke a poet made about his own luck. He goes on: if he dealt in burial shrouds, nobody would die as long as he lived. Whatever he tried, the world arranged itself so that he couldn't make a living. The man who wrote that was not a failure. He was a sharp-eyed reader of the Bible, a grammarian, an astronomer, a poet, and a wanderer who carried his books from city to city. Today, Abraham ibn Ezra.
screen: `CANDLES, AND THE SUN NEVER SETS.` → `A POET LAUGHS AT HIS LUCK.` → `A WANDERER WITH BOOKS.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ezra grew up in Muslim Spain, in the world of the poets we've met this week. Then he left, and kept moving: Italy, France, and, by his own writings, as far as England. Wherever he stayed, he wrote. Spanish Jewish learning had grown up in Arabic, and Arabic was not the language of the Jews of Christian Europe. So ibn Ezra did something simple and huge: he wrote it out in Hebrew. Grammar books, astronomy, and above all commentaries on the Bible. As a commentator he wanted the plain meaning of the words, what Hebrew calls peshat. He paid close attention to grammar, how a verb is built, why a word is spelled the way it is. He could be blunt with interpretations he thought ignored the words on the page. And he had a sharp eye for the odd detail. Here is one. When Abram first arrives in the land, Genesis says, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "And the Canaanite was then in the land." Then? Ibn Ezra noticed that little word. He wrote that there is a secret here, and that the one who understands it should keep silent. He doesn't say what the secret is. Readers have argued ever since about what he meant. Some read it as a hint about who wrote that line and when; others read it differently. That is very ibn Ezra: sharp, brief, and willing to leave a question hanging. A traveler learns to notice what locals stop seeing. Maybe that is why he saw so much in a word like then. He carried his books everywhere, and left behind commentaries that Jews still print beside the Torah.
screen: `A WANDERER: ITALY, FRANCE, ENGLAND.` · `SPANISH LEARNING CARRIED INTO HEBREW.` · `PESHAT: THE PLAIN MEANING.` · then, large: `AND THE CANAANITE WAS THEN IN THE LAND.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: read one commentary. Settle, and let your breath slow. Take the verse we just heard: and the Canaanite was then in the land. Say it once, slowly. Now read it the way ibn Ezra did. Which word stops you? Why that word and not another? What question would you write in the margin? You don't need an answer. Just notice the question. Later, if you have a minute, find one commentary on any verse you like and read it beside the verse. If you pray, you can ask in your own words to read with open eyes. The bell holds the time.
Ibn Ezra. A wandering poet, grammarian and Bible commentator from Spain who looked for the plain meaning, peshat, in every verse. Today's word.
Your line: the traveler. Today, look at one familiar place, your street, your kitchen, your commute, as if you had just arrived, and notice one detail you stopped seeing. Day nine hundred twenty-six.

927.title: Maimonides' life
927.hook: born in Córdoba, he fled persecution and became a physician in Cairo
927.howItsDone: Jews around the world study the Rambam's Mishneh Torah, some following a daily study cycle, and his Thirteen Principles appear in prayer books in the form of the hymn Yigdal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abraham ibn Ezra: poet, grammarian, and a commentator who never stayed long in one city. Your line was the traveler. What detail did you notice that you had stopped seeing? Today, another traveler, though not by choice. Day nine hundred twenty-seven.

A student wanted to visit a busy man in Egypt, and the man wrote back a warning: come if you like, but don't expect a long talk. Then he explained. Each morning he went to the palace as a doctor. When he rode home, his hallway was already full: Jews and non-Jews, officials and ordinary people, all waiting to see him. He took one quick meal, then treated them until night. That picture comes from the letter itself. The same man wrote a code of Jewish law that people still study and a book of philosophy that people still argue about. And he did not start out in Egypt at all. He started out in Spain, in Córdoba, and a long road of flight lies between the two. Today, the life of the Rambam.
screen: `A DOCTOR'S CROWDED HALLWAY.` → `A LETTER TO A STUDENT.` → `CÓRDOBA TO CAIRO.`

segments.voice: Rambam is a name built from initials: Rabbi Moshe ben Maimon. English speakers often call him Maimonides, son of Maimon. His father was a judge and scholar in Córdoba, and the boy grew up in that learned city. Then the ground shifted. A new ruling movement, the Almohads, took power in Muslim Spain and North Africa and pressed Jews and Christians to convert or leave. The family chose the road. They moved from place to place in Spain, then crossed to Fez in Morocco, then sailed east to the land of Israel, and finally settled in Fustat, the old city of Cairo. Consider what that meant for a young scholar. Books carried in bags. Teachers left behind. No settled home for years. And yet he kept writing the whole way, a commentary on the Mishnah begun on the move. In Egypt he became a physician, and in time a doctor to the court. He also led the Jewish community, answered legal questions in letters, and finished his great code of law, the Mishneh Torah, and later his philosophy book, the Guide for the Perplexed. Here is a thread worth holding. The Torah keeps reminding a people who had been strangers how to treat strangers. In the JPS translation of Deuteronomy: "Love ye therefore the stranger; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." The Rambam had been a stranger in many lands. He ended up in Egypt itself, and his door was open to whoever came.
screen: `RAMBAM: RABBI MOSHE BEN MAIMON.` · `CONVERT OR LEAVE: THE FAMILY LEAVES.` · `FEZ, THE LAND OF ISRAEL, FUSTAT.` · then, large: `LOVE YE THEREFORE THE STRANGER.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: learn one refugee's story. Settle first, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind someone who had to leave a home: a grandparent, a coworker, a neighbor, a family in the news, or the Rambam's family on the road. Hold their route in your mind, one place at a time. What did they carry? What did they leave? Who opened a door for them? Later today, if you can, ask someone their story and just listen, or read one account in their own words. If you pray, you can hold them in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Rambam. Rabbi Moshe ben Maimon, also called Maimonides: a refugee from Córdoba who became a doctor, a teacher of law and a philosopher in Egypt. Today's word.
Your line: from córdoba to cairo. Today, notice one person who is far from where they started, and make their day a little easier. Day nine hundred twenty-seven.

928.title: The letter to Yemen
928.hook: Maimonides writes to encourage persecuted Jews in Yemen
928.howItsDone: The letter to Yemen is studied today as an example of Jewish leadership in hard times, and Yemenite Jews have long honored the Rambam's writings and memory.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rambam: a family on the road, and a doctor's hallway full of patients in Egypt. Your line was from córdoba to cairo. Whose story of leaving home did you hear? Today, a letter he sent south. Day nine hundred twenty-eight.

The news from the far south of Arabia is bad. It comes to Egypt in a letter from Jacob, a leader of the Jews of Yemen. A new ruler there is pressing Jews to convert. Some have given in. A preacher who had converted is telling people their own scriptures point to his faith. And in one town a man has stood up claiming to be the messiah, and people are following him. Jacob is asking a stranger far away what to tell his frightened community. The man he wrote to had once been a refugee from that very kind of pressure. Today, the letter that came back.
screen: `BAD NEWS FROM YEMEN.` → `PRESSURE, DOUBT, A FALSE MESSIAH.` → `A QUESTION SENT NORTH.`

segments.voice: The answer is known in Hebrew as Iggeret Teiman, the letter to Yemen. The Rambam wrote it in Arabic, the everyday language of his readers, so that ordinary people could follow it, not only scholars. And it is warm. He opens with praise for Jacob and for the community, and he does not scold the ones who are wavering. Then he takes their three troubles one at a time. The pressure first. He tells them that hard times have come before, and that the people have outlasted them before; he asks them to hold on to the covenant and not lose heart. Then the doubt. To the claim that their own books point somewhere else, he answers that the verses are being bent out of their meaning, and he urges them to keep studying their own texts. Then the false messiah. He tells them gently but firmly that this man is not who he says he is, and that following him puts the whole community in danger. He judges that the man seems unwell in his mind, and advises the community to deal with him quietly, for its own safety. And near the end he asks for something practical: copy this letter and read it aloud in every community, so no one is left alone with the bad news. The language of courage runs back to the Torah itself. As Moses tells the people in the JPS translation of Deuteronomy: "Be strong and of good courage." Tradition says the Jews of Yemen held this letter dear, and remembered its writer in their prayers. A frightened community wrote to a stranger, and the stranger wrote back as a friend.
screen: `WRITTEN IN ARABIC, FOR EVERYONE.` · `PRESSURE, DOUBT, A FALSE MESSIAH.` · `READ IT ALOUD IN EVERY COMMUNITY.` · then, large: `BE STRONG AND OF GOOD COURAGE.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: write one encouraging note. Settle, and breathe slowly. Think of one person carrying something hard right now: an illness, a job loss, a lonely stretch, a fear they've told you about. Let their face come clear. Now, in your head, start the note the way the Rambam started his: with something true and good about them. Then one plain line of support. No advice unless they asked. When the bell ends, write it down and send it, on paper or on your phone. If you pray, you can hold them in your own words first. The bell holds the time.
Iggeret Teiman. The Rambam's letter to Yemen, written in Arabic so ordinary people could follow it, meant to be read aloud to a frightened community. Today's word.
Your line: write to encourage. Today, send the note you started, and make the first sentence about what is good in them. Day nine hundred twenty-eight.

929.title: His brother David
929.hook: his brother drowned at sea on a trading voyage; Maimonides grieved for years
929.howItsDone: Jewish mourning moves in stages, with shiva in the first week, shloshim through the first month, a year of saying Kaddish for a parent, and a yahrzeit candle lit on each anniversary of the death.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the letter to Yemen: a warm answer to a frightened community, written to be read aloud. Your line was write to encourage. Did your note go out? Today, a letter of a different kind, about the Rambam's own loss. Day nine hundred twenty-nine.

Two brothers, one house. The older one, Moses, sits with his books. The younger one, David, packs for a long trip. He is a merchant, and the family lives on what he earns. That arrangement is what lets his brother study and write without worrying about bread. David sets out by sea, heading for India, carrying his own money and money that others have trusted him with. And then the ship goes down. Today, the brother of the Rambam, and what the Rambam himself wrote about his grief.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS, ONE HOUSE.` → `A MERCHANT SAILS FOR INDIA.` → `THE SHIP GOES DOWN.`

segments.voice: We know this mostly from the Rambam's own words. Years later he wrote a letter to an old friend, a judge in the land of Israel who had traveled with him once. The friend had complained that the Rambam had not written in a long time. The answer is deeply personal. He explains that the worst thing that ever happened to him was the death of his brother, who drowned in the Indian Ocean. He says that for about a year afterward he lay ill, in grief, close to despair. He says David had been raised on his knees, that they had studied together, that David had carried the family's business so that he could stay at his desk. David left a young widow and a little daughter, and the Rambam took them in. Then comes the line that gives today its name. Even now, he writes, after all this time, he is still mourning. When he sees David's handwriting or one of his books, the grief comes back. Notice who is saying this. This is the writer of a vast code of law and a demanding book of philosophy, a man who wrote about the mind and its control of feeling. And he does not pretend. He tells his friend plainly that the loss still lives in him. Jewish mourning has its own rhythm: the first week, the first month, the first year, and the yearly day of remembrance after that. The rhythm does not say grief ends. It gives grief a shape to walk through. The Rambam's letter shows a scholar walking through it slowly, and saying so.
screen: `A LETTER TO AN OLD FRIEND.` · `DROWNED IN THE INDIAN OCEAN.` · `HE STILL MOURNED, YEARS LATER.` · then, large: `GRIEF GIVEN A SHAPE.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: remember a sibling or a friend. Settle, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind someone close to you, someone you shared a house with, or a childhood, or a long friendship. They may be living or gone. Picture one ordinary thing about them: their handwriting, a laugh, the way they packed a bag. Stay with that picture. If grief comes, let it sit beside you; it doesn't need fixing. If they're living, think of one thing you'd like them to know. If you pray, you can remember them in your own words. The bell holds the time.
David. The Rambam's younger brother, a merchant lost at sea, still mourned years later in his brother's own letter. Today's word.
Your line: grief takes years. Today, reach out to one person who lost someone a while ago, when the calls have stopped, and simply say you remember. Day nine hundred twenty-nine.

930.title: Nachmanides
930.hook: a Catalan rabbi who defended Judaism at the Barcelona disputation, then settled in the land of Israel
930.howItsDone: The Ramban's Torah commentary is printed in study editions of the Bible alongside Rashi and Ibn Ezra, and a synagogue in Jerusalem's Old City bears his name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, his brother David: lost at sea, and still mourned years later in the Rambam's own letter. Your line was grief takes years. Did you reach out to someone? Today, a name that sounds almost the same, one letter apart. Day nine hundred thirty.

Rambam, yesterday. Ramban, today. One letter changes, and it is a different man, born about two generations later, in a different country. Moshe ben Maimon became the Rambam. Moshe ben Nachman became the Ramban, and in English, Nachmanides. He lived in Girona, in Catalonia, a doctor and a rabbi, and he wrote a commentary on the Torah that is still printed in study editions today. One day a summons came. The king of Aragon wanted him in Barcelona, in the royal palace, to answer questions about his faith in public, against a man who had been born Jewish and become a Christian friar. He could not refuse.
screen: `RAMBAM, RAMBAN: ONE LETTER APART.` → `A RABBI IN GIRONA.` → `A SUMMONS TO BARCELONA.`

segments.voice: The debate is called the Barcelona disputation. The friar, Pablo Christiani, argued that passages in the rabbis' own writings showed the messiah had already come. The Ramban was asked to respond, in front of the king and church leaders. Picture the risk. A rabbi speaking freely about another faith, before the powerful, could put his whole community in danger. So before he began, according to his own account, he asked the king for one thing: permission to speak freely. The king granted it. What we know comes mostly from the Ramban's own written report, and there is also a short Latin record from the other side, and the two don't tell it the same way. That is worth saying plainly. Each side wrote down its own version. What stands out in the Ramban's account is his manner. He answers point by point, from the texts. He says that stories in the Talmud and the midrash are not all binding in the same way as law. He is direct, at times sharp, and he is respectful of the king, who, he writes, sent him home with a gift. Afterward, his account was published, and he faced trouble for it. In time he left Catalonia and made the journey to the land of Israel. In a letter home to his son, he describes Jerusalem as poor and desolate, and tells how he helped gather a few people and set up a place to pray. Strength of argument, without contempt. And when the pressure grew, a new beginning far away.
screen: `ASKED TO ANSWER IN PUBLIC.` · then, large: `PERMISSION TO SPEAK FREELY.` · `POINT BY POINT, FROM THE TEXTS.` · `A NEW START IN JERUSALEM.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: stand for what you believe, with dignity. Settle, and breathe slowly. Think of one conversation coming up where you'll need to hold your ground, at work, at home, online. Before the words, find the manner. The Ramban asked for the freedom to speak, then spoke from his sources, without mocking anyone. What is the one thing you want to say clearly? What's the one thing you won't say, because it would only wound? Hold both. If you pray, you can ask in your own words for a steady voice. The bell holds the time.
Ramban. Rabbi Moshe ben Nachman, called Nachmanides: a Torah commentator from Girona who answered in public at Barcelona, then went to Jerusalem. Today's word.
Your line: defend with dignity. Today, when you disagree with someone, make your point from what you know, and leave out the jab. Day nine hundred thirty.

931.title: The Zohar
931.hook: in Castile, Moses de León circulates the Zohar, the book of radiance
931.howItsDone: Some Jews study the Zohar in groups or read a portion daily, and its teachings shaped customs like the Friday night Kabbalat Shabbat service and some Sabbath songs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Ramban: summoned to Barcelona, asking for the freedom to speak, then a new start in Jerusalem. Your line was defend with dignity. Did you leave out the jab? Today, the end of the week, and a book wrapped in light. Day nine hundred thirty-one.

In a town in Castile, a scholar named Moses de León starts sending out pages. Copies, he says, of an old book. It is written mostly in Aramaic, a language of the Talmud, and it reads like a long walk through the Torah with a circle of ancient teachers, led by a rabbi of the Mishnah, Shimon bar Yochai. They stop on a verse, and one of them opens it, and the verse turns out to have rooms inside rooms. Scholars, students and mystics begin copying the pages. The book has a one-word name: Zohar.
screen: `PAGES SENT OUT FROM CASTILE.` → `ARAMAIC, LIKE THE TALMUD.` → `A VERSE WITH ROOMS INSIDE.`

segments.voice: The name comes from a verse in the book of Daniel. In the JPS translation: "And they that are wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament." Brightness there is zohar. So the title means radiance, splendor, a light that shines. And the book is about hidden light. The Zohar reads the Torah as having a surface and a depth. The stories and laws are the garment; underneath is a soul. It speaks of the sefirot, ways that the hidden God is revealed in the world, and it imagines human actions, a prayer, a kind deed, a Sabbath meal, as echoing up through those worlds. Now the honest part: who wrote it? There are two answers, and people hold them sincerely. Traditional readers receive the Zohar as the teaching of Shimon bar Yochai and his companions, handed down and later brought to light. Other readers, historians among them, look at its language and its world and conclude it was composed in Castile in the time of Moses de León, by him or by a circle around him. There is even an old account of a traveler, Isaac of Acre, who went looking for the ancient original and heard conflicting answers. Both views agree on what happened next. The Zohar became a central book of Kabbalah, Jewish mystical teaching. Its ideas flowed into prayer books and Sabbath songs and into later movements of the spirit. People still sit with it slowly, a line at a time, the way its own teachers sit with a verse.
screen: `ZOHAR: BRIGHTNESS, FROM DANIEL.` · then, large: `SHALL SHINE AS THE BRIGHTNESS OF THE FIRMAMENT.` · `A GARMENT AND A SOUL.` · `WHO WROTE IT? TWO ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: read one line of mystical writing. Take the verse the book is named for, and go slowly. And they that are wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament. Breathe in on the first half, out on the second. Say it once more, more slowly. Then ask the Zohar's kind of question: what is under the words? What makes a person shine? Who in your life has had that kind of brightness? Let the line sit in you without solving it. If you pray, you can carry the verse into your own prayer. The bell holds the time.
Zohar. Brightness, radiance, from a verse in Daniel: the name of a central book of Jewish mysticism, written mostly in Aramaic and circulated from Castile. Today's word.

Your line: the book of radiance. Looking back this week: the greater war is inside, a traveler, the Rambam's road and his letters, the Ramban's dignity, and now hidden light. Today, find one brightness in an ordinary person. Day nine hundred thirty-one.

original.note: Hebrew: brightness, radiance, as in Daniel's 'brightness of the firmament'.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Zohar is a book of secret spells.
what it means: it is a mystical reading of the Torah, finding a soul beneath the words and a hidden light in the world.
what a scholar hears: written mostly in Aramaic, named from Daniel, received by tradition from Shimon bar Yochai and dated by some historians to Castile.
